name: Fast C++ CSV Parser
workload: Reading a generated 8-column CSV (id,city,state,category,amount,quantity,flag,note) of 500K or 5M rows with clean and quoted-field profiles, in a count-rows loop and a full read loop into std::string cells, warm cache, single parser worker, Google Benchmark median real time.
claimed_speedup: Single-parser-worker raw read, median real time (csv-parser vs fast-cpp-csv-parser): 500K clean count 146.5 ms vs 81.8 ms (~1.8x, derived from page data), read 164.9 ms vs 82.8 ms (~2.0x, derived from page data); 500K quoted count 197.2 ms vs 118.8 ms (~1.7x, derived from page data), read 223.5 ms vs 136.2 ms (~1.6x, derived from page data); 5M clean read 1,087 ms vs 944.2 ms (~1.15x, derived from page data). Reversed at 5M rows elsewhere: 5M clean count 547.6 ms for csv-parser vs 881.5 ms, 5M quoted count 665.4 ms vs 1,153 ms, 5M quoted read 1,140 ms vs 1,164 ms (csv-parser ahead). csv-parser also wins both materialization tables (e.g. 5M clean 739.6 ms vs 2,105 ms) and the positional-read table once it uses 4+ speculative parser workers (500K clean spec-4 76.6 ms vs fast-cpp SPSC 88.0 ms).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0, C++20, CMake Release configuration (MSVC Release defaults; no extra optimization flags in benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), /arch:AVX2 added to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS by csv-parser's top-level CMakeLists.txt on MSVC (in csv-parser's own directory scope, so the fast-cpp benchmark executables in benchmarks/ probably build without it), CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark 1.8.5
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12400 (12 logical CPUs, ~2.5 GHz), Windows 11 Home 25H2, Samsung 990 EVO SSD
tradeoffs: Single header csv.h. Column count and types are fixed at compile time (read_header plus read_row with typed arguments), so there is no dynamic row model. Does not parse quoted fields with embedded line breaks (the comparison marks the multiline profile unsupported). Optional background I/O thread (needs pthread with GCC, or CSV_IO_NO_THREAD). The caller owns row materialization and any parallelism.
caveats: The benchmark is in the competitor's repo (csv-parser author), not the project's own, and it was written to show where csv-parser wins: fast-cpp-csv-parser wins only at 500K rows and the 5M clean read, and loses the 5M count rows (clean and quoted), the 5M quoted read, both materialization tables and the 4+ worker positional-read comparison. The two read harnesses do different work: fast-cpp's 'count rows' still copies all 8 fields into std::string per row while csv-parser's count only iterates rows, and fast-cpp's 'read' copies all 8 fields while csv-parser takes 3 string_views by column name; fast-cpp is configured with double_quote_escape and trim_chars even on the clean profile. Windows/MSVC only, one machine, Google Benchmark overhead included. The fast-cpp-csv-parser source is fetched with FetchContent GIT_TAG master, so no commit is pinned (the repo has not changed since 2025-02-02). Optimization flags are implied by CMake Release rather than listed. fast-cpp-csv-parser cannot parse quoted line breaks (multiline profile skipped). The project's own README has no numbers, and no measurement against the guessed std::getline baseline was found (dfglib's csvPerformanceRuns.md only compares it with dfglib's own readers). [retier] Third-party competitor harness (vincentlaucsb/csv-parser benchmarks/README.md, 'CMake Release', unpinned master): wins only the 500K and 5M clean-read rows and loses 5M count, 5M quoted read, materialization and 4+ worker reads; the csv-parser targets get /arch:AVX2 through a PUBLIC compile option while the standalone fast-cpp binary gets no AVX2, and the result JSON shows the 500K wins mostly measure csv-parser start-up cost (csv-parser count 196 MB/s at 500K vs 543 MB/s at 5M, fast-cpp flat at 315-350 MB/s). Harnesses differ (fast-cpp copies all 8 fields). Correctness: the float parser is not correctly rounded (issue #122), empty numeric cells silently become 0, the real line limit is 2^20 (block_len) not 2^24-1, and the default reader has no quote handling. Last commit 2025-02-02.

name: Vince's CSV Parser
baseline: fast-cpp-csv-parser (also rapidcsv and Glaze's CSV reader in the same suite)
workload: Google Benchmark median real time on a generated 8-column CSV (id,city,state,category,amount,quantity,flag,note) of 500K and 5M rows in clean, quoted and multiline profiles: raw row count/read, one-pass row materialization, materialize plus multi-pass aggregation, and DataFrame load and load+edit+save against rapidcsv.
claimed_speedup: Median real time, generated 8-column CSV, own harness. Single-worker comparisons hold only for the 500K inputs (28.7 MB, under the 50 MB speculative-parallel threshold): materialization 156.8 ms vs fast-cpp-csv-parser 218.8 ms (about 1.4x, derived from page data) and materialize plus multi-pass aggregation 215.4 vs 237.1 ms and 262.9 vs 280.7 ms (about 1.1x, derived from page data); rapidcsv DataFrame load 1.48x at 500K multiline (220.4 vs 325.2 ms). The 5M rows (297-445 MB) ran csv-parser with speculative parallel parsing (speculative_parallel_threads=0, auto = 12 hardware threads) against single-threaded baselines: materialization 739.6 vs 2,105 ms (2.8x), quoted 930.6 vs 2,489 ms (2.7x), materialize plus aggregation 1,251 vs 2,252 ms (1.8x) and 1,517 vs 3,090 ms (2.0x), rapidcsv 3.45-4.53x, Glaze 739.6 vs 1,972 ms; the explicit single-worker 5M read took 1,442 ms in the same session. Positional read with 4 speculative workers 702.2 ms vs 915.1 ms (spec-8 605.0 ms). Loses the small raw reads (500K clean count 146.5 vs 81.8 ms, read 164.9 vs 82.8 ms) and the multi-pass-only step on materialized rows (5M clean 479.5 vs 141.6 ms).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0, C++20 (Glaze targets C++23), CMake Release configuration (MSVC Release defaults; benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt adds no optimization flags), /arch:AVX2 added as a PUBLIC compile option of the csv library target in include/internal/CMakeLists.txt (so it reaches every benchmark binary that links csv, but not the standalone fast_cpp_csv_parser_* and glaze_csv_* binaries), CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark v1.8.5 via FetchContent; fast-cpp-csv-parser and rapidcsv fetched at unpinned master, Glaze v7.5.0
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12400 (12 logical CPUs, about 2.5 GHz), Windows 11 Home 25H2, Samsung 990 EVO SSD
tradeoffs: Fully RFC 4180-compliant out of the box (embedded newlines, quoted fields), which fast-cpp-csv-parser does not support and which costs raw throughput. Dynamic row model with string-valued fields and optional type conversion rather than compile-time typed columns. Fast paths use memory-mapped files and a speculative parallel parser (after Ge et al., SIGMOD 2019) with a background thread, 10 MB default chunks, so it uses more cores and more memory than a single-threaded streaming reader. C++11 minimum, C++20 recommended; ships a DataFrame and a CSV writer.
caveats: Project's own benchmarks, one machine, one OS and one compiler (Windows 11, MSVC 19.50), result JSON dated 2026-05-08 while the library has changed since (last commit 2026-10-06), so ordering may shift on GCC/Clang, Linux or newer code. The 'materialization' tables compare different amounts of work: csv-parser pushes CSVRow handles that keep parser-owned buffers alive and parse fields lazily on get<>, while fast-cpp-csv-parser copies six std::string fields and converts two integers per row into a struct (and Glaze deserializes into reflected structs); the cost shows up later, where csv-parser's multi-pass step on materialized rows is 3.4x slower (479.5 ms vs 141.6 ms at 5M clean). The fairer materialize+aggregation table still favours csv-parser, by about 1.1x at 500K rows and 1.8-2.0x at 5M rows. Flag asymmetry: /arch:AVX2 is a PUBLIC option of the csv target, so csv-parser binaries (and both libraries inside csv_parser_fast_cpp_read_bench) build with AVX2 while the standalone fast_cpp_csv_parser_* and glaze_csv_* binaries build with the MSVC default ISA. fast-cpp-csv-parser wins the 500K raw read and count tests; csv-parser times grow sublinearly from 500K to 5M rows (count 146.5 to 547.6 ms), so fixed start-up cost dominates the small runs. The rapidcsv comparison pits csv-parser's filename path (memory-mapped reader with its background worker thread on, CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON) against rapidcsv's single-threaded Document. Comparison libraries are fetched at unpinned master (fast-cpp-csv-parser, rapidcsv). No comparison against std::getline or any libstdc++/libc++ code was found. 'Likely one of the fastest general-purpose C++ CSV ETL libraries' is the author's wording. Inputs are generated, not real-world data (the README's Kaggle-file timings, such as 1.4 GB in about 0.5 s on warm cache, have no baseline). [retier] Project's own benchmarks on one machine, OS and compiler (Windows 11, MSVC 19.50 Release, /arch:AVX2 as a PUBLIC option of the csv target with no runtime dispatch, so only csv-parser binaries get AVX2; i5-12400; results dated 2026-05-08). The README labels the materialize, ETL and rapidcsv tables single-parser-worker, but bench_format() leaves speculative_parallel_threads=0 (auto = hardware_concurrency, 12) with a 50 MB threshold, so every 5M input ran speculative parallel parsing against single-threaded baselines; the 500K inputs are the only like-for-like rows. The materialization tables also compare different work: csv-parser pushes lazy CSVRow handles while fast-cpp-csv-parser copies six std::string fields and converts two integers per row, and csv-parser's later multi-pass step on materialized rows is 3.4x slower. Same defaults in 92fe668 (5.0.0, 2026-05-08).

compiler_and_flags: gcc 14 -O3 (CMake Release build driven by bench/run_bench.sh), libcurl 8.14 (system libcurl, also used by cpr via CPR_USE_SYSTEM_CURL=ON), asio 1.38; cpr 1.11.2 and cpp-httplib v0.20.0 pinned via FetchContent in bench/CMakeLists.txt; Debian 13 on WSL2; nginx from bench/nginx.conf (4 workers, keep-alive, access log off) on the same host

tradeoffs: Header-only (needs libcurl and ASIO), C++17, C++20 coroutines optional; callbacks, futures and coroutines from one implementation; libcurl gives HTTP/2, TLS and connection pooling. Needs an asio::io_context to drive it. Very new repo (first commit 2026-07-10).
caveats: First-party benchmark with public code (bench/) but the CPU model is not stated, so tier C. The headline is asynchronous (100 requests in flight on one thread) against synchronous clients with one request in flight, so the single-thread win measures concurrency, not a faster HTTP client. In the 20-thread tier cofetch splits 100 in-flight requests over 20 loops (5 each) while the cpr and cpp-httplib pools keep only 20 in flight, so 'equal-sized thread pools' still gives cofetch 5x the concurrency; those runs last only 0.12-0.16 s. The README's 'wins every scenario' is contradicted by its own RTT rows: at 10 ms RTT one cofetch thread only ties 100-thread pools (cpp-httplib's pool is 2% faster) and at 50 ms RTT the pools are about 5% faster (derived from page data). In the sequential chain the README uses the busy-poll mode: in the default run() mode cofetch (11,116 req/s) and its coroutine form (10,547 req/s) are slower than cpp-httplib (12,761 req/s), and the page says so. Loopback to a local nginx sharing the WSL2 host, not a real network; run-to-run variance about +/-10% per the page. Compared to cpr both sit on libcurl. The page also reports an internal epoll baseline about 14% faster than cofetch on loopback. The numbers (2026-07-10) predate commit c1bd40f (2026-09-29), which fixed leaked in-flight easy handles at Client destruction, resolver descriptors ignored by socket_cb and multi-block header parsing, and added transfer-node recycling; none of these affect the IP-literal, redirect-free benchmark's correctness, but the published numbers are from older code. name: SafeRE
workload: JMH microbenchmarks: 150-row real-world matrix (25 patterns x match/no-match x 1K/10K/100K input sizes), plus 8 'Core' and 8 'Application' workloads, run against java.util.regex (JDK), RE2/J, RE2-FFM (Java FFM binding to native C++ RE2), native C++ RE2, PCRE2 JIT, Go regexp, Rust regex crate, and .NET's non-backtracking engine.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 2.22x faster than JDK java.util.regex on the 150-row real-world matrix (1.88x without the 2 pathological backtracking rows), but 22% slower than JDK on Core and 7% slower on Application. 12.5x faster than RE2/J and 3.06x faster than RE2-FFM on the real-world matrix. Against native engines on the real-world matrix, SafeRE is 13% slower than C++ RE2 (150 rows), takes 2.03x as long as Rust regex (150 rows) and 2.47x as long as PCRE2 JIT (only 48 supported rows). It is 1.32x faster than native RE2 on Core.
compiler_and_flags: Java: OpenJDK 26.0.2+10-55 targeting Java 21, JMH 1.37 (2 forks, 2 warmup iters x500ms, 5 measurement iters x500ms); C++: g++ 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG, RE2 snapshot 2025-11-05; PCRE2 10.47 with JIT enabled; Go 1.26.1 linux/amd64; Rust rustc 1.97.1 with regex 1.13.1; .NET SDK 10.0.110
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K, 8 cores/16 threads, 3.6 GHz base, 16 GiB RAM under WSL2, Ubuntu 24.04 on Windows 11 host, Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2
tradeoffs: 71.2x slower to compile a pattern than the JDK (11.7x slower than RE2/J), and retains substantially more memory per compiled pattern, in exchange for guaranteed linear-time matching with no catastrophic-backtracking risk (e.g. 0.089us vs the JDK's 17,079us on an adversarial pattern). Cross-runtime ratios mix FFI/marshalling overhead with engine cost, so they are not pure same-runtime comparisons.
caveats: SafeRE is a from-scratch Java port of RE2's design (not a GitHub fork), so is_fork_of is null even though it is explicitly 'based on RE2'. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION because the LICENSE file is a compound notice, but the file text states both RE2 and RE2/J (and by extension this port) are BSD-3-Clause. Critically, on the primary 150-row real-world matrix, SafeRE is NOT faster than any of the three named baselines it tested that are on our incumbent list (RE2, PCRE2, Rust regex) -- it is slower than all three there; its clear win is only over java.util.regex, which is a widely used incumbent but not one of PCRE2/RE2/std::regex/Rust regex. This is an unusually rigorous, self-critical benchmark report (authors explicitly flag their own losses), which raises confidence in the numbers despite the mixed result.

On the extended benchmarks (Fig. 5b) RE# is first overall (1.09 vs Hyperscan 3.77, rust/regex 29.5), 'often by several orders of magnitude'. RE# is not fastest in every category: rust/regex has lower slowdown in baseline categories 6.1.1 literal/literal-alternate (1.49 vs 1.98) and 6.1.3 (1.38 vs 1.43). The numbers are in Deepparse's docs (docs/source/parser.rst); that page does not cite a paper for the timing tables (its arXiv link, 2006.16152, is the 2020 accuracy paper). Search snippets (snippet only; arXiv and ACL Anthology blocked) say the NLP-OSS 2023 paper 'Deepparse: An Extendable, and Fine-Tunable State-Of-The-Art Library for Parsing Multinational Street Addresses' (arXiv 2311.11846, ACL Anthology 2023.nlposs-1.3) reports the same experiment in Tables 1-2 on an RTX 2080 GPU and states that libpostal had the better inference time. The benchmark code is public in GRAAL-Research/deepparse models_evaluation/: libpostal was timed through the pypostal Python binding (postal.parser.parse_address in a Python loop over ~183,000 addresses, wall-clock time.time()), not from C, and both runs are wrapped in memory_profiler's @profile, whose line tracing adds overhead to the libpostal loop, so the libpostal figure is if anything pessimistic. The committed speed_test_evaluation.py calls process_fn() without its batch_size argument and reopens its result file inside the batch loop, so it cannot have produced the Deepparse rows as written; its 'batch of more than 1' column is the mean over batch sizes 2 to 512, not the best batch. name: libucl
workload: Parse and emit a 19 MB JSON file of about 700 thousand lines generated with json-generator.com, timing the whole-file parse and each emit format.
claimed_speedup: Parse: jansson 1.3899 s vs UCL 0.6649 s (about 2.1x, derived from page data); UCL built with -O3 parses in 0.3002 s (about 4.6x vs the jansson figure, derived from page data, but the jansson figure is not stated to be -O3). Emit: jansson 0.2609 s vs UCL config 0.2423 s, JSON 0.2329 s, compact JSON 0.1811 s, YAML 0.2489 s (about 1.1x for JSON, derived from page data); UCL -O3 emit 0.1174 s config and JSON, 0.0991 s compact JSON, 0.1354 s YAML.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the jansson run. The first UCL set is described only as unoptimized, the second as 'compiled with optimizations (-O3)'.
tradeoffs: UCL is a configuration language that is a superset of JSON (macros, includes, variables, comments, implicit arrays, multiple values per key, JSON Schema v4 validation) with CBOR and MessagePack input and output, so the parse does more than plain JSON. The README warns that with all features enabled it is meant for trusted configuration input only and must not take adversarial input. C API with an object tree; zero-copy parsing is an opt-in flag (UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY). Bindings for Lua, Python and Haskell live in the repo.
caveats: First-party README numbers from one run on one generated 19 MB JSON file: no CPU, OS, compiler version, jansson version or jansson build flags are given, and the two UCL sets differ in optimization level (the first is unoptimized, the second -O3), so the ratios mix builds. tests/test_speed.c (2013 copyright header, so the numbers are probably old) times only UCL: it mmaps the file, uses UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY and times ucl_parser_add_chunk plus ucl_parser_get_object with clock_gettime; the jansson harness is not in the repo, and the README's 'make check' suggestion runs only UCL. Whether the quoted run used zero-copy is not said; zero-copy favours UCL over jansson, which allocates its own strings. The emit gap against jansson is small (about 1.1x for JSON). The only evidence is JSON parsing and emitting, not UCL's own config syntax or YAML/TOML/XML parsing against the category's baselines (libyaml, yaml-cpp, toml++, libxml2, pugixml). No independent benchmark including libucl was found. [retier] First-party README numbers (parse 0.6649 s vs jansson 1.3899 s) unchanged since tag 0.2.0 (2013-12-03), before the uthash-to-klib switch in 0.7.0; one run each, mixed -O levels, JSON-only evidence. test_speed.c starts the timer after mmap and parses ZEROCOPY while speed.test pre-reads the file ('Preread file to cheat benchmark!'); the jansson harness, version and flags were never published. Workload is public: tests/rcl_test.json.xz (19,001,364 bytes, 693,050 lines), best figure about 63 MB/s (-O3, derived). Many open fuzzer-found memory-safety issues (#352 ZEROCOPY use-after-free with add_file, #388, #387, #367); the hash seed defaults to time(NULL) through an unsynchronized static.
